pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Shapes of land and water (landforms & water bodies)

- **Standards — UK (KS1/KS2 Geography — use basic geographical vocabulary for physical features; use maps and simple models):** Children name and describe landforms (mountain, valley, hill, plain, cliff) and water bodies (river, lake, ocean, pond) and represent an area's features on a simple map/model.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-ESS2-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-2].

- **Operational details:** Two joined goals: (1) a vocabulary of physical features — mountain, valley, hill, plain, cliff; river, lake, ocean, pond — each pinned to its defining shape (a valley is a low dip between higher land; a plain is flat and wide); and (2) the modelling skill of representing those features for a real area on a map or relief model, understanding that a map is a bird's-eye stand-in for the real place. Use photographs to build the words, then a map or a built model (sand tray, salt-dough relief, blue for water) so children translate 3D land into a 2D/scaled representation. Emphasise that models leave out detail but keep the shapes and positions that matter.
bestPractices: Pin each landform/water word to its defining SHAPE using photographs before mapping (valley = dip between highlands, plain = wide and flat).
Move from real place → model: build a sand tray or salt-dough relief, or draw a map, so children translate 3D land into a scaled representation.
Make the map's conventions explicit — bird's-eye view, blue = water, and that a model keeps shapes/positions but drops detail.
Contrast confusable pairs (hill vs mountain; lake vs pond; river vs lake) by their defining features.
Have children model THEIR local area or a story's setting so the representation maps to something real to them.
keyRepresentations: Photo cards of landforms and water bodies matched to their names.
A simple map (bird's-eye) with blue water and shaded relief.
A physical relief model (sand tray, salt dough) of an area.
A landform–description matching set (mountain ↔ 'very high, steep land').
commonMisconceptions: 'A map shows what you see standing there' — not grasping the bird's-eye/top-down view.
'Hill and mountain are the same' (or lake and pond) — not distinguishing by size/height.
'Rivers and lakes are the same because both are water' — missing that a river flows and a lake is still.
'The blue on a map is the sky' — not reading blue as water.
'A model is a toy, not a representation' — not seeing the model as standing for a real place.

learn.summary: For 7–8 year-olds learning the shapes of land and water: pin each landform and water-body word to its defining shape using photographs, then have children build or draw a simple model/map of a real area so they translate 3D land into a scaled, bird's-eye representation. The culminating goal (NGSS 2-ESS2-2 / KS1-2 Geography) is developing a model that keeps key features and their positions while deliberately dropping detail. A vocabulary scene, matching/sorting checks, and 3D terrain sculpting are complementary approaches with different purposes.

activities.title: Build a map of an area from land and water features
feedback: If the river is drawn running uphill or away from lower water, ask: which way does water flow? Trace from the high mountains down to the lowest water body.
When a learner matches the top-down map to the side-on relief, confirm that the blue squiggle on the flat map is the same river seen from above.
If a child worries the model is 'wrong' because it is small or missing trees, affirm that a good model keeps the important features and their arrangement and drops the rest on purpose.
activities.rationale: The standard asks learners to develop a model of land and water in an area, so active composition plus linking top-down to side-on views turns passive naming into representation and shows how features relate. An optional interactive builder that nudges a river toward the lowest water, and a toggle between bird's-eye and relief views, make this mechanism concrete; a physical sand/salt-dough build serves the same goal hands-on. Efficacy of any specific builder is untested and proposed only.
sourceClaims: KS1/KS2 geography: use basic geographical vocabulary for key physical features and use maps and simple models to represent places.
learnerActions: Compose an area by placing landform pieces (a mountain range along one edge, hills, a valley between higher land, a flat wide plain, a cliff) and water pieces (a lake in a hollow, a river, an ocean at an edge).
Draw or lay down a river so it runs downhill from the mountains, through the valley, into the lake and on towards the sea.
Label each feature in place as it is added.

Switch or compare between the bird's-eye (top-down) map and a side-on relief view of the same area, so the flat blue line you drew for the river becomes a river threading the valley in the relief model.
As a hands-on complement, build a salt-dough or sand-tray relief of your own local area (blue for water) and then draw its bird's-eye map.
activities.intendedInsight: A map is the same land seen from directly above; features connect sensibly (water flows downhill, so a modelled river runs toward lower water), and a model keeps the shapes and positions that matter while leaving out detail.

activities.title: Name and compare landforms and water bodies from photographs
feedback: For 'river vs lake', prompt: does the water flow along a long channel, or mostly stay in one hollow? A river flows along from higher to lower land; a lake's water mostly stays in one place, even if it has small waves.
For 'hill vs mountain', compare height and steepness with clear side-by-side examples.

In a photograph, if a child mixes up blue water with the sky, use position and shape to tell them apart: a water body sits low in the land (a hollow, valley or at the coast), while the sky is above the horizon. (The separate convention that blue means water on a map is covered in the map-reading activity.)
activities.rationale: Pinning vocabulary to defining shapes with real photographs builds the naming half of the goal and pre-empts confusable-pair misconceptions. This activity supports vocabulary strongly; recognition on its own does not elicit the build-a-model skill the standard foregrounds, so pair it with a construction task.
sourceClaims: KS1/KS2 geography: use basic geographical vocabulary for key physical features and use maps and simple models to represent places.
learnerActions: Explore a rich landscape scene (or photo cards) containing a mountain, valley, hill, plain, cliff, river, lake, ocean and pond.
Reveal each feature's name and its defining shape (valley = a low dip between higher land; a plain = flat and wide).

Answer shape-comparison prompts that contrast confusable pairs: 'mountain or hill?' (height/size), 'lake or pond?' (size), 'river or lake?' (a river flows along a long channel; a lake's water mostly stays in one hollow, though it may have waves and streams flowing in or out).
activities.intendedInsight: Each landform and water-body word is tied to a defining shape or behaviour, not just a label, so similar features can be told apart.

activities.title: Sort and match features; read a simple map
feedback: If a learner calls the blue area on the map 'sky', remind them that on a map blue stands for water and the view is looking straight down from above.
If land/water sorting slips, revisit the defining feature of each item.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising and single map-reading questions give a clean check of naming and classification. This checks recognition and classification; it does not by itself require the learner to construct a model, so pair it with a build/draw task.
learnerActions: Match photographs to landform/water names (e.g. mountain ↔ 'very high, steep land').
Categorise features as land or water.
Read a simple bird's-eye map and answer: 'what is the blue area on this map?'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can classify features and begin reading map conventions (bird's-eye view, blue = water).

activities.title: Sculpt 3D terrain and flip to its map (extension)
feedback: After sculpting, ask the child to look straight down at their terrain and compare what they see to the flat map.
Check that raised land and hollows on the model correspond to the right places on the map.
Note that a physical clay/sand relief has real thickness and only approximates the land, whereas the flat map is its top-down representation; neither is the real place.
activities.rationale: Hands-on or 3D terrain work is genuinely spatial and may strengthen the link between 3D land and a 2D map. For this age the core targets are met in 2D, so treat 3D as a rich extension that offers a different experience rather than a required mechanism; its added benefit over 2D is not established here.
learnerActions: Raise a mountain, carve a valley, and flood a lake in a manipulable 3D terrain (physical modelling clay/sand, or a screen model).
Then view or draw the same terrain's flat bird's-eye map to connect the 3D shape to its top-down representation.
activities.intendedInsight: The same piece of land can be experienced as a 3D shape and as a 2D map; the map records the shapes and positions seen from above.

constraints: Cover at least four landforms (mountain, valley, plain, hill, cliff) and at least three water bodies (river, lake, ocean, pond).
Make map conventions explicit: bird's-eye/top-down view, blue = water, and that a model keeps shapes and positions but drops detail on purpose.
Anchor at least one modelling task to something real to the child (their local area or a story's setting).

Matching, sorting and single-answer map questions assess recognition and classification; they do not on their own require the learner to construct a model, so pair them with a build/draw task to meet the standard.
A tappable naming scene builds vocabulary but does not by itself elicit the build-a-model skill; use it alongside a construction activity.

Treat 3D terrain sculpting as an optional extension, not a requirement; a physical cutout or relief has real thickness and approximates the land, while a flat map is the top-down representation of it.
Present the river rule as the age-appropriate heuristic 'water flows downhill' (so a modelled river runs toward lower water), not as an invariant of all real drainage.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were not re-fetched or re-verified, and the listed sources are marked verified:false in the source row.
Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions; no claim of tested effectiveness is made.

The 'river runs downhill to the lowest water body' rule is a sound simplification for this age: water flowing downhill under gravity is physically correct, but the claim that a river always reaches the lowest water body on the map is a modelling heuristic, not an invariant of all real drainage; present it as 'water flows downhill'.
Original recommendation leaned on a specific interactive drag-and-place builder; the generic builder/physical-model goal is preserved while product-specific framing is removed.
Source confidence was legacy-marked 'high'; this rewrite does not upgrade or re-verify that confidence.

The omitted 'conversation' alternative carried a categorical 'dialogue would merely list landforms' claim; it is dropped as a non-teaching option rather than reproduced as a medium-superiority judgement.

probeDeeper: If your model doesn't show every house and tree, does that make it useless? Why or why not?
How is a mountain different from a hill on your model?
Someone new to the area uses your map. What should it help them do?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes, it can still be a good model. A model or map represents where things are and their shapes — not every detail — and it doesn't have to be full size. Its job is to show the arrangement of land (hills, valleys, plains) and water (rivers, lakes) so you can understand the area or find your way around it.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A model is only good if it looks exactly like the real thing and shows everything'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A model keeps the important features and their positions and leaves out the rest on purpose.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a bad model because it's small and missing the trees.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: rejects a simplified or scaled-down model

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A map is just a picture from the side' — can't handle the top-down view
errorPatterns.nextMove: Practise looking straight down on a model, then match it to the map.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: struggles to read a bird's-eye map

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A hill and a mountain (or a lake and the ocean) are the same thing'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort features by size and shape with clear examples.
errorPatterns.distractor: A hill and a mountain are just the same thing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can't distinguish landform or water-body types

responseLevels.gap: Insists a model must be full-size or show everything; can't name or distinguish features.
responseLevels.full: Names and distinguishes several land and water features, builds or reads a simplified model/map, and explains that a model represents the arrangement of key features rather than every detail.
responseLevels.partial: Names landforms and water bodies and makes a model but thinks it must copy reality exactly, or can't say what the model is for.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You make a model (or map) of your local area showing a hill, a river and a lake. Your model is much smaller than the real place and doesn't show every tree. Is it still a good model? What is a model or map actually for?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks a model must look exactly like reality or be the same size differs from one who understands a model represents the key features and their positions.

sources.claim: KS1/KS2 geography: use basic geographical vocabulary for key physical features and use maps and simple models to represent places.
